key_terms.meaning: The peak arterial pressure, in mmHg, reached just after the ventricles contract
The lowest arterial pressure, in mmHg, just before the next contraction
The tapping sounds heard through a stethoscope over the brachial artery as cuff pressure falls below systolic
MAP ≈ diastolic pressure + (systolic − diastolic)/3, in mmHg
Cardiac output CO = 60 I / A: dye mass I (mg) ÷ area A under the first-pass curve (mg·s/L), the Stewart–Hamilton relation
Cardiac output from the temperature drop seen downstream after injecting a known volume of cold saline
First heart sound, from closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole
Second heart sound, from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole
A recording of heart sounds and murmurs, usually shown with a simultaneous ECG for timing
A two-channel recording of foetal heart rate and uterine contraction, used in labour
Forced vital capacity: the total volume of air, in litres, blown out as hard and fast as possible after a full breath in
The volume, in litres, exhaled in the first second of a forced expiration
Fraction of the forced vital capacity expelled in one second; normally about 0.75 to 0.80 in adults
Body temperature (37 °C), ambient pressure, saturated with water vapour; lung volumes are reported under these conditions
A flow sensor that reads the small pressure drop across a fixed resistance and converts it to flow
The pressure in the thin space between lung and chest wall, normally slightly below atmospheric
Arterial oxygen saturation from the ratio of ratios R of red and infrared pulsatile light; SpO₂ ≈ 110 − 25R (%) as a textbook line
Breathing measured from the change in electrical impedance across the chest as air enters and leaves the lungs
The volume of air, in litres, left in the lungs after the deepest possible expiration
R<sub>aw</sub> = (alveolar pressure − mouth pressure) ÷ flow, in cm H₂O per L/s
V<sub>tg</sub> = ΔV × (P<sub>B</sub> − 47 mmHg) / ΔP<sub>mouth</sub>; equals FRC when the shutter closes at end-expiration
[(P<sub>B</sub> − P<sub>w</sub>)/(P<sub>B</sub> − 47)] × 310/(273 + t), about 1.08 at 24 °C

takeaways: Blood pressure is a pressure above atmosphere, so a catheter transducer is zeroed to air at heart level; the cuff method reads it indirectly from Korotkoff sounds (phase I systolic, phase V diastolic) or from the peak of cuff oscillations (MAP).

Dilution gives cardiac output as indicator dose ÷ area under the first-pass curve: CO = 60 I / A for dye, and the same idea with heat for thermodilution; recirculation must be cut off by extrapolating the exponential decay.
Heart sounds are low-frequency events from valve closure (S1, S2) and ventricular filling (S3, S4); a phonocardiogram is timed against the ECG R wave to find systole and diastole.

A foetal monitor must cancel the mother's larger ECG or use Doppler before it can count the baby's rate; an arrhythmia monitor turns each RR interval into a rate, and one missed QRS halves the rate it reports.
Spirometry gives volumes and flows (FVC, FEV1, their ratio) corrected from ATPS to BTPS; it cannot measure residual volume or FRC.
A pneumotachometer turns a small laminar pressure drop into flow and integrates it to volume; alveolar and pleural pressures are found indirectly, by brief interruption and by an oesophageal balloon.
A pulse oximeter forms the ratio of ratios R from red and infrared AC/DC signals; it reports saturation, not ventilation, and is fooled by carbon monoxide, motion and poor perfusion.
Impedance pneumography and apnoea monitors watch the timing of breathing, not its volume, and alarm after a set silent time of 10 to 20 s.

The body box applies Boyle's law to the gas trapped in the chest during panting to give FRC, RV and airway resistance; helium dilution and nitrogen washout give FRC from gas balance but miss trapped gas.
bank_note: Long answers are asked on the working principle, the block diagram and the sources of error of each instrument, usually with one numerical question on dilution cardiac output, BTPS correction or lung volumes. The respiratory instruments (spirometer, pneumotachometer, body plethysmograph, apnoea monitor) are the core of the exam course.

bank.q: Define systolic, diastolic and mean arterial pressure. Describe the auscultatory method of indirect blood pressure measurement and explain what produces each phase of the Korotkoff sounds.
outline: Pressure is measured relative to atmosphere, in mmHg
Cuff placed on upper arm, inflated above systolic to stop flow
Cuff deflated slowly at 2-3 mmHg per second
Turbulent flow under the cuff produces phase 1 tapping sound = systolic
Sound muffling (phase 4) and disappearance (phase 5) = diastolic
Cuff must be at heart level to avoid hydrostatic error
MAP = diastolic + (systolic - diastolic)/3
Sources of error: cuff size, observer hearing, deflation rate
answer: Definitions. Blood pressure is the pressure in an artery above atmospheric, in mmHg. Systolic pressure S is the peak in each beat, just after the ventricles eject; diastolic pressure D is the lowest value, just before the next beat. Mean arterial pressure is the time-average that perfuses the organs: MAP ≈ D + (S − D)/3 at normal heart rates, because diastole lasts about twice as long as systole.

Equipment. A cloth cuff holds an inflatable bladder about 40 % of the arm circumference wide and 80 % long; a bulb and valve inflate and deflate it; a mercury or aneroid manometer shows cuff pressure; a stethoscope (or a microphone in automated units) sits over the brachial artery below the cuff. The cuff is at heart level, with the arm supported.

Procedure. (1) Inflate about 30 mmHg above the pressure at which the radial pulse disappears, so the artery is fully shut and silent. (2) Deflate at 2–3 mmHg per second. (3) Note the cuff pressure at the first clear tapping sound (systolic) and where the sounds vanish (diastolic). (4) Deflate fully and wait before repeating.

answer.text: Korotkoff phases and their cause. When cuff pressure falls just below systolic, the artery opens for a moment at the peak of each beat; blood squirts through the narrowed segment as a turbulent jet and the wall snaps open, which is heard as a tap. As the cuff falls further the artery stays open for longer in each beat and the sound changes:

head: Phase
Sound
Cause
Reading (example)
rows: artery opens only at the peak of each beat
longer opening, turbulence below the cuff
larger volume of blood per beat strikes the wall
artery closes only briefly near diastole
artery stays open all through the beat; flow is laminar

answer.text: Worked numbers. With 160 mmHg inflation and 3 mmHg/s deflation:
answer.pre:
time to first sound  = (160 − 128) / 3 = 10.7 s
pulse pressure       = 128 − 82 = 46 mmHg
MAP                  = 82 + 46/3 = 97.3 mmHg
systolic in kPa      = 128 × 0.1333 = 17.1 kPa

answer: Phase IV or V. Phase V is used as diastolic in adults. In children, pregnancy and aortic regurgitation the sounds may go on to zero cuff pressure; then phase IV is recorded and the reading is written as, for example, 128/100/0.

Sources of error. A narrow cuff reads high and a wide cuff low; an arm 10 cm below the heart reads about 8 mmHg high (0.78 mmHg per cm of blood); deflating faster than 3 mmHg/s misses the true first and last sounds; an auscultatory gap in some hypertensive patients can make the observer miss systolic unless the palpatory pressure is found first; observer hearing and digit preference add bias.
Check. MAP of 97.3 mmHg lies between D = 82 and S = 128 and nearer to D, as it must when diastole is the longer phase.

bank.q: Explain the origin of the four heart sounds and describe a phonocardiograph recording system, including the choice between the bell and diaphragm of a stethoscope.
outline: S1 from mitral and tricuspid closure at start of systole
S2 from aortic and pulmonary closure at end of systole
S3 early diastolic filling sound, S4 late diastolic atrial sound
Microphone, low-noise amplifier, band-pass filter of about 20–500 Hz with selectable bands
Simultaneous ECG for timing
Bell picks up low frequencies, diaphragm filters them out for higher murmurs
Systole is the interval between S1 and S2, diastole between S2 and the next S1
answer: Origin of the four sounds. S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole (components M1, T1); it is the longer, lower sound. S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole (A2, P2); it is shorter and sharper, and splits on inspiration because P2 is delayed. S3 is a low sound in early diastole as blood rushes into the ventricle; it is normal in children and young adults. S4 is a low sound in late diastole when the atrium contracts into a stiff ventricle; it usually indicates disease in an adult.

Frequency content. S1 and S2 have most energy below about 200 Hz; S3 and S4 are below about 50 Hz; murmurs, from turbulence, reach several hundred hertz. A recording system therefore needs a band of about 20–500 Hz with selectable sub-bands.

Stethoscope: bell and diaphragm. The stethoscope couples chest-wall vibration to the ear; it does not amplify. The bell is an open cup, held lightly, that passes low frequencies: use it for S3, S4 and the rumble of mitral stenosis. Pressing it hard stretches the skin into a membrane and the low sounds fade. The diaphragm is a stiff membrane, pressed firmly, that suppresses low frequencies and brings out S1, S2 and high-pitched murmurs such as aortic regurgitation. Short, wide, thick-walled tubing keeps losses small.

answer.text: Phonocardiograph block diagram.
answer.pre:
chest microphone → preamplifier → band-pass filter → amplifier → recorder / display
                                     ↑
                         ECG lead II channel (time reference)

answer: Blocks. The microphone is air-coupled (a small chamber over a capacitive or electret element) or a contact piezoelectric type. The preamplifier has a high input impedance so it does not load the crystal. The filter rejects baseline wander and body movement below about 20–25 Hz and noise above the chosen upper cutoff; a narrow band gives a clean trace but can hide a high-frequency murmur. A simultaneous ECG channel is essential: the R wave marks electrical activation, so S1 and S2 can be timed against it.

answer.text: Timing example. S1 starts 0.05 s and S2 0.35 s after an R wave; the next R wave is at 0.80 s.
answer.pre:
systole  = 0.35 − 0.05 = 0.30 s
diastole = 0.80 − 0.30 = 0.50 s
heart rate = 60 / 0.80 = 75 beats per minute

answer: Reading the trace. A murmur between S1 and S2 is systolic; between S2 and the next S1 it is diastolic. A 600 Hz murmur would be largely removed by a 25–400 Hz filter, so the band must suit the question being asked.
Check. Systole (0.30 s) plus diastole (0.50 s) equals the RR interval (0.80 s), and diastole is the longer phase at 75 beats per minute, as expected.

bank.q: Describe the dye dilution and thermal dilution methods of cardiac output measurement. Give the working equation and list the assumptions.
outline: Indicator injected upstream, concentration sensed downstream
Stewart-Hamilton: CO = amount injected / (mean concentration x time base)
Dye such as indocyanine green, measured by densitometry at the ear or artery
Thermal dilution uses cold saline and a thermistor on a pulmonary artery catheter
Recirculation removed by extrapolating the exponential decay on semilog paper
Indicator must mix completely and be lost only by flow
Thermal method needs correction for heat loss to catheter wall
Sources of error: injection loss, recirculation, unstable flow
answer: Principle. A known amount of indicator is injected upstream and mixes with all the blood passing; downstream its concentration c(t) is recorded. Mass balance: everything injected passes the sensor once, so I = Q ∫c dt. Hence Q = I / ∫c dt, and in L/min, CO = 60 I / A, where A is the area under the first-pass curve in mg·s/L. Older books write this as CO = I / (c̄ × t), with c̄ the mean concentration over the curve duration t.

Dye dilution. Indocyanine green (about 5 mg) is injected quickly into a central vein. Arterial blood is drawn through a densitometer cuvette that reads optical absorption near 800 nm. The curve appears after a few seconds, peaks, falls almost exponentially, and then a second hump appears as dye recirculates. The downslope is plotted on semilog paper and extended as a straight line; the area under the measured part plus the extrapolated tail is A.

answer.text: Worked numbers (dye). Samples every 2 s from 4 to 16 s: 0, 3.0, 7.5, 6.0, 4.2, 3.0, 2.1 mg/L.

answer: Thermal dilution. A Swan-Ganz catheter floats through the right heart into the pulmonary artery. A known volume of cold 5 % dextrose or saline (10 mL at 0–4 °C) is injected through the proximal port in the right atrium; a thermistor near the tip records the fall in blood temperature. The equation replaces dye mass with heat: CO = 60 VI(TB − TI)K1 / ∫ΔT dt, with K1 ≈ 1.08 for dextrose. For 10 mL at 2 °C, blood at 37 °C and an area of 4.5 °C·s: CO = 60 × 0.010 × 35 × 1.08 / 4.5 = 5.04 L/min.

Assumptions. (1) The indicator mixes completely with all the flow before the sensor. (2) None is lost between injection and sensor (for heat: the catheter wall warms the injectate, so a correction constant is used). (3) Flow is steady over the measurement (breathing changes it, so readings are averaged). (4) The whole first pass is recorded and recirculation is excluded.

Comparison. Thermal dilution needs no dye, gives no dye accumulation, and can be repeated every few minutes; its signal is small, so iced injectate is used for a better signal-to-noise ratio. Dye dilution needs arterial sampling and a densitometer and becomes harder to repeat as background dye builds up.

Errors. Slow or leaking injection; wrong computation constant for the volume or temperature used; recirculation counted in the area (makes CO low); valve regurgitation or shunts that break the single-pass assumption.
Check. Both methods give about 5 L/min, the normal resting adult value, and CO falls when A rises, as the equation demands.

bank.q: Draw and explain a normal forced expiratory spirogram. Define FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC and FEF25-75, and state how the shape separates obstruction from restriction.
outline: Volume-time curve: steep first second, then plateau
FVC = total volume exhaled after full inspiration
FEV1 = volume in first second
Normal FEV1/FVC about 0.75–0.85 in young adults; below 0.70 (or the lower limit of normal) means obstruction
Obstruction: low ratio because FEV1 falls more than FVC
Restriction: normal or high ratio but both FEV1 and FVC reduced
FEF25-75 is the average flow over the middle half of the breath, sensitive to small-airway disease
Flow-volume loop shapes: scooped in obstruction, narrowed in restriction
answer: The test. The subject breathes in to total lung capacity and blows out as hard and fast as possible for at least 6 s through a spirometer, nose clipped. The volume-time curve is the forced expiratory spirogram.

answer.text: Normal spirogram. A steep rise in the first second (most of the air leaves early, at high flow), then a curve that flattens to a plateau at FVC. In the normal subject of the example 3.2 L of a 4.0 L FVC is out in the first second.

svg.aria: Spirogram: normal curve to 4.0 L with FEV1 3.2 L; obstructive curve to 3.0 L with FEV1 1.2 L

answer: Definitions. FVC is the total volume exhaled in the forced manoeuvre. FEV1 is the volume exhaled in the first second. FEV1/FVC is their ratio (dimensionless). FEF25–75 is the mean flow over the middle half of the exhaled volume, from 25 % to 75 % of FVC; it falls early in small-airway disease but varies with effort.

answer.text: Numbers from the curves.

answer: Obstruction. Narrowed airways slow the air out, so FEV1 falls much more than FVC and the ratio drops below 0.70 (or below the lower limit of normal for age, sex and height). The curve rises slowly and may not plateau by 6 s; the flow-volume loop shows a low peak and a scooped expiratory limb.

Restriction. A small, stiff lung empties quickly through open airways: FVC and FEV1 both fall but the ratio is normal or high, the curve is a small copy of the normal one, and the flow-volume loop is narrow and tall-shaped. Spirometry only suggests restriction; a low TLC from a body box or helium dilution confirms it.
Technique. Volumes are corrected from ATPS to BTPS (factor about 1.08 at 24 °C); the best of three acceptable blows within 0.15 L of each other is reported.

Flow-volume loop. The same blow plotted as flow against volume shows the difference more clearly: the normal loop rises at once to a peak of 8–10 L/s and falls in a nearly straight line to FVC; the obstructive loop has a low peak and a concave, scooped descent; the restrictive loop is narrow (small FVC) but its peak and slope are near normal or high for its size.

FEF25–75 in the example. For the normal subject the middle half of the 4.0 L is from 1.0 L to 3.0 L exhaled; if that takes 0.55 s, FEF25–75 = 2.0 L / 0.55 s = 3.6 L/s. A smoker with a normal ratio but an FEF25–75 well below predicted may have early small-airway disease.
Check. In the asthma case FEV1 is 1.2/3.0 = 40 % of FVC against 80 % in the normal subject, so the ratio, not FVC, marks the obstruction.

bank.q: An indicator dilution curve is recorded after injecting 5 mg of dye. The mean concentration over the curve is 2.5 mg per litre and the curve base lasts 12 s. Calculate cardiac output in litres per minute and comment on whether the value is physiological.
outline: CO = amount / (mean concentration x time)
Convert time to minutes: 12 s = 0.2 min
Resting adult value is about 5 L/min, so 10 L/min is high
High output suggests exercise, sepsis, anaemia or a left-to-right shunt
Check injection loss, curve extrapolation and calibration
answer: Formula. Stewart–Hamilton: CO = I / (c̄ × t), where I is the dye mass, c̄ the mean concentration over the curve and t the curve duration. The product c̄ × t is the area A under the curve.

Where the formula comes from. All of the dye passes the sampling site once. In a small time dt a volume Q dt of blood passes, carrying c Q dt of dye. Adding over the whole first pass: I = Q ∫c dt = Q × c̄ × t, so Q = I / (c̄ t). The mean concentration times the duration is simply the area under the curve.

answer.text: Working.

answer: Same answer with seconds. A = 2.5 × 12 = 30 mg·s/L, so CO = 60 × 5 / 30 = 10 L/min. Use one time unit throughout: multiplying by 60 when the area is already in mg·min/L would give 600 L/min.

Is it physiological? A resting adult has about 5 L/min (heart rate 70 × stroke volume 70 mL = 4.9 L/min). 10 L/min is twice that: normal during moderate exercise, but at rest it suggests a high-output state such as fever, sepsis, severe anaemia, thyrotoxicosis or an arteriovenous shunt.

Check the measurement first. (1) Was all 5 mg delivered? A leak at the injection port lowers the real dose, but the calculation still uses 5 mg, so CO reads high. (2) Was the curve cut off too early, missing tail area? A smaller A gives a higher CO. (3) Was the densitometer calibrated with the patient's own blood and dye standards? A calibration error scales c̄ directly.

Stroke volume. If the heart rate at the time was 100 per minute, stroke volume = 10 000 mL/min ÷ 100 = 100 mL, above the resting 70 mL; a rate of 140 would give 71 mL, so a high output at rest is more often a fast heart than a bigger stroke.
Check. Halving the area to 15 mg·s/L would double CO to 20 L/min; doubling it to 60 would give the normal 5 L/min, so the result depends on the area exactly as the equation says.

bank.q: A spirometer calibrated at ATPS reads 3.00 L for a forced vital capacity at 25 °C and 750 mmHg. Describe how the reading is converted to BTPS and explain why the correction is needed. Also list the checks a 3 L calibration syringe is used for.
outline: BTPS = body temperature 37 °C, ambient pressure, water vapour saturated
Gas expands as it warms from 25 °C to 37 °C
Corrected FVC = 3.00 × 1.075 = 3.22 L
Reason: the lung reports volumes at body conditions, so clinic readings must match
Syringe used to check linearity, leaks, and volume accuracy of the sensor
Also check that a known 3 L push reads about 3 L on the display
answer: Why correct. Gas in the lungs is at body temperature (37 °C), ambient pressure and saturated with water vapour (BTPS). When it is exhaled into a spirometer at room temperature it cools and some water vapour condenses, so the same gas fills a smaller volume (ATPS). Predicted values and lung volumes are quoted at BTPS, so the reading must be scaled up.

answer.text: Formula.

answer: P<sub>B</sub> is barometric pressure (750 mmHg), P<sub>w</sub> the saturated vapour pressure at the spirometer temperature (23.8 mmHg at 25 °C), 47 mmHg the vapour pressure at 37 °C, and 310 K body temperature.

answer.text: Working.

answer: Meaning. Without the correction the patient's FVC would be reported 0.22 L (7 %) low, enough to move a borderline result below the lower limit of normal.

Calibration syringe. A 3.000 L syringe is emptied through the spirometer before each session. It checks (1) volume accuracy: the reading must lie within about ±3 % (2.91–3.09 L) — note that the syringe gas is at room conditions, so no BTPS factor is applied to this check; (2) leaks in a volume-displacement spirometer, by holding the syringe pushed in against a closed outlet; (3) flow linearity of a flow-sensing spirometer, by emptying the syringe at slow, medium and fast speeds and getting 3 L each time.

Order of the corrections. The temperature term alone (1.040) accounts for most of the change; the pressure term (1.033) adds the volume of water vapour that evaporates into the gas as it warms to 37 °C. At 37 °C both terms become 1 and the factor is exactly 1, which is a quick way to check the formula has been written the right way up.
Check. The factor is larger than 1, as it must be when gas warms from 25 °C to 37 °C, and close to the usual 1.07–1.10 range for room temperature.

bank.q: A screen pneumotachometer has a resistance of 0.5 cm H₂O per L/s and shows a pressure drop of 1.5 cm H₂O. Find the flow. Explain how the signal is made linear and how volume is obtained from it.
outline: Flow = pressure drop / resistance = 1.5/0.5 = 3 L/s
Flow is proportional to pressure drop only when the flow profile is laminar (Poiseuille)
Capillary or screen element keeps flow laminar
Two symmetric pressure taps allow bidirectional measurement
Flow is electronically integrated to give volume
Drift of the integrator needs a reset or a high-pass zero
Gas condition affects viscosity, so BTPS correction applies
answer: Flow. For a linear pneumotachometer ΔP = R × Q, so Q = ΔP / R = 1.5 / 0.5 = 3 L/s.

Construction. A screen pneumotachometer holds a fine wire mesh across the breathing tube; a Fleisch head uses a bundle of parallel capillaries. Pressure taps on each side of the element feed a differential pressure transducer, whose bridge output is amplified by a carrier amplifier.

Why it is linear. Poiseuille's law says the pressure drop across a tube is proportional to flow while flow is laminar. The mesh or capillaries divide the stream into many small channels with a low Reynolds number, so the flow stays laminar over the working range. Above it, turbulence adds a term in Q² and the reading rises faster than flow; the remedy is a larger head or a stored linearisation curve.

Keeping it linear in use. Symmetric taps and a symmetric element give the same calibration for inspiration and expiration. The element is heated a few degrees above body temperature so exhaled water does not condense on the mesh and raise R. The calibration is checked with known steady flows (for example 0.5, 1 and 2 L/s giving 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 cm H₂O).

answer.text: Volume from flow. The flow signal is integrated electronically or numerically:
answer.pre:
V = ∫ Q dt
example: Q = 3 L/s held for 0.5 s → V = 1.5 L

answer: Drift. Any zero offset is integrated too: an offset of 0.01 L/s adds 0.6 L in a minute. The integrator is reset at the start of each breath, or a measured zero is subtracted.
Gas conditions. Viscosity changes with gas composition and temperature, so R changes; exhaled gas is warmer and wetter than the calibration air, so volumes are corrected to BTPS.

Back-pressure on the patient. At 3 L/s the element adds 1.5 cm H₂O of resistance, small beside the normal airway resistance of about 1–2 cm H₂O per L/s times the same flow, so the subject barely notices it. A head with a resistance of 2 cm H₂O per L/s would add 6 cm H₂O at this flow and change the breathing it is meant to measure.
Check. (1.5 cm H₂O) ÷ (0.5 cm H₂O per L/s) = 3 L/s; the units cancel to L/s, as a flow must, and 3 L/s is a normal peak flow for quiet panting or a moderate exhalation.

bank.q: A two-wavelength pulse oximeter measures the ratio of ratios R = 0.6. Explain how R is formed, how it is converted to SpO2, and describe three situations in which the reading becomes unreliable.
outline: Red and infrared LEDs alternately illuminate the finger
Photodiode current has a steady and a pulsatile part
Ratio uses the pulsatile (AC) divided by steady (DC) part at each wavelength
R = AC/DC at red divided by AC/DC at infrared
R is mapped to SpO2 through a calibration curve from volunteer studies
Unreliable with poor perfusion, motion artefact, nail polish or bright light
Carboxyhaemoglobin and methaemoglobin read falsely high or low
answer: Light path. A red LED (about 660 nm) and an infrared LED (about 940 nm) are switched on in turn, hundreds of times per second, on one side of a finger; a photodiode on the other side measures the light that gets through. A transimpedance amplifier converts the photocurrent to a voltage and a demultiplexer separates the red and infrared channels.

AC and DC. Skin, bone, tissue and venous blood absorb a steady amount: the DC level. Each heartbeat adds a little arterial blood, which lengthens the path through arterial blood and makes the transmitted light dip: the AC part. Low-pass filtering gives DC, band-pass filtering at the heart rate gives AC.

answer.text: Ratio of ratios. Dividing AC by DC in each channel cancels the LED brightness and the steady tissue absorption; dividing the red ratio by the infrared ratio leaves a number that depends on the colour of arterial blood:

answer: Why it tracks saturation. At 660 nm reduced haemoglobin absorbs far more than oxyhaemoglobin; at 940 nm oxyhaemoglobin absorbs slightly more. As saturation falls, the red pulsation grows and the infrared pulsation shrinks, so R rises.

answer.text: Conversion to SpO₂. R is mapped through an empirical curve measured in volunteers; textbooks use the straight line SpO₂ ≈ 110 − 25R.

answer: Three situations that make it unreliable. (1) Poor perfusion (cold hands, shock, vasoconstrictors): the AC part becomes tiny and noise dominates. (2) Motion artefact: movement changes the path length in both channels and imitates a pulse, so R and the reading are wrong. (3) Carbon monoxide poisoning: carboxyhaemoglobin absorbs red light like oxyhaemoglobin, so SpO₂ reads falsely high. Methaemoglobinaemia (reading drifts towards 85 %), dark nail polish and strong ambient light also corrupt the reading.
Check. R = 0.6 is above the 0.55 that gives 96 %, so the estimate must be below 96 %: 95 % is consistent.

bank.q: Compare direct and indirect methods of blood pressure measurement. Discuss which is chosen in an intensive care unit, in a home check-up, and during exercise testing, giving reasons.
outline: Direct: catheter in artery with strain-gauge or fluid-coupled transducer, continuous waveform, gold standard
Direct risks: infection, thrombosis, bleeding, needs trained staff
Indirect: cuff with auscultation, oscillometry or ultrasound, non-invasive, intermittent
Indirect errors: cuff size, arrhythmia, calcified arteries, observer bias
ICU uses direct arterial line for beat-to-beat values and drug titration
Home and clinic use automated oscillometric cuff devices
Exercise testing needs fast repeated readings, so automated cuffs or finger methods are used
Conclusion: choice depends on need for continuity, accuracy and risk
answer: Direct method. A cannula in the radial (or femoral) artery connects through a stiff, bubble-free saline line to a strain-gauge diaphragm transducer zeroed to air at the level of the right atrium. A bridge amplifier and monitor show the full waveform beat by beat, with systolic, diastolic and mean values. The line must be flushed continuously, and its natural frequency and damping must be adequate: low damping overshoots (systolic high), a bubble lowers the natural frequency and blunts the peaks.

Indirect methods. (1) Auscultatory: cuff, manometer and stethoscope, Korotkoff phase I and V. (2) Palpatory: systolic only, from the return of the radial pulse. (3) Doppler ultrasound: detects returning flow, useful in infants and in shock. (4) Oscillometric: a pressure sensor in the cuff records the oscillations; maximum oscillation gives MAP and fixed amplitude ratios give systolic and diastolic.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Feature
Direct (arterial line)
Indirect (cuff)
rows: one reading every 1–2 min at best
±5–10 mmHg; cuff size, arm level, observer

answer: Intensive care unit. Direct. Patients on vasopressors, in shock or under anaesthesia need beat-to-beat pressure to titrate drugs, and the arterial line also allows repeated blood gas samples. The systolic difference between radial line and cuff (134 against 128 mmHg in the example) is expected from peripheral amplification; the means agree within 1 mmHg.

Home check-up. Indirect, with an automated oscillometric upper-arm monitor of validated design: no skill needed, repeatable morning and evening, and it avoids the white-coat effect of clinic readings. The cuff must fit the arm and the arm must be supported at heart level.

Exercise testing. Indirect. A line is rarely justified, but movement and treadmill noise ruin oscillometric readings, so an automated auscultatory unit with a microphone and ECG gating (listening only in a window after each R wave), or a trained observer, is used; readings are taken every 2–3 minutes.

Accuracy check of a cuff device. A new automated monitor is validated against careful auscultatory readings by two trained observers on a set of subjects; the mean difference should be within about ±5 mmHg with a standard deviation under about 8 mmHg. Such a device can then replace the observer in the clinic and at home.
Conclusion. The choice weighs the need for continuous data against invasiveness: direct where every beat matters and risk is accepted, indirect everywhere else.

bank.q: Describe a foetal monitoring system based on abdominal ECG and phonocardiography. Explain how the foetal signal is separated from the maternal signal and how the arrhythmia monitor in the same unit measures RR intervals.
outline: Abdominal electrodes pick up both maternal and foetal ECG
Foetal R wave is smaller; maternal complexes are removed by subtraction or gating
Foetal heart rate computed from foetal RR interval, about 110-160 beats per minute
Ultrasound Doppler and foetal phonocardiography are alternatives
Cardiotocograph plots foetal rate against uterine contractions
Arrhythmia monitor measures each RR interval and compares with running average
Alarm when rate crosses limits or RR changes abruptly
Artefacts: movement, electrode loss, missed R waves; need blanking and averaging
answer: Signals available. On the mother's abdomen electrodes pick up both maternal and foetal ECG. The maternal QRS is about 5–10 times larger and comes at 60–100 per minute; the foetal QRS is small (often 10–50 µV) and comes at 110–160 per minute.

answer.text: Block diagram.
answer.pre:
abdominal electrodes → isolated bio-amplifier (high CMRR) → band-pass filter
  → maternal QRS detector → cancel (subtract template or blank window)
  → foetal QRS detector → RR interval → rate meter → CTG chart with uterine pressure

answer: Separating the signals. (1) Subtraction: a maternal chest lead (or the abdominal signal averaged over many maternal beats) gives a maternal QRS template, which is scaled and subtracted at each maternal beat. (2) Logic (blanking): a window of about 100 ms around each maternal QRS is blanked, and foetal peaks are taken only outside it; a foetal beat hidden inside the window is filled in from the running foetal rate. Adaptive filters are the modern form of subtraction.

Phonocardiography and Doppler. A microphone on the abdomen picks up foetal heart sounds; a filter rejects the maternal sounds and bowel noise, and the rate is counted from S1. A 1–2.5 MHz Doppler transducer gives an audible shift from the moving heart walls (about 390 Hz for 0.15 m/s at 2 MHz); its envelope repeats at the foetal rate. Both are passive and non-invasive; a scalp electrode after membrane rupture gives the cleanest direct foetal ECG.

Rate. FHR = 60 / Tf; at 140 per minute Tf = 0.429 s. The cardiotocograph prints foetal rate above uterine pressure: baseline 110–160 per minute, variability 5–25 per minute, accelerations, and early, variable or late decelerations.

Arrhythmia monitor. One ECG lead is band-pass filtered (about 5–15 Hz) to favour the QRS; a threshold or slope detector marks each R wave; the time between R waves is the RR interval and Rinst = 60/RR. Each RR is compared with the running average and with set limits: tachycardia (for example above 120 per minute), bradycardia (below 50), pause (RR above 1.5–2 s) and asystole. Premature beats are flagged when RR is short and the QRS is wide.

answer.text: The missed-beat error.
answer.pre:
true RR = 0.80 s → 60/0.80 = 75 per minute
one QRS missed → measured RR = 1.60 s → 60/1.60 = 37.5 per minute → false pause alarm

answer: Artefacts and remedies. Movement and electrode loss (lead-off detection, signal-quality index); maternal QRS mistaken for foetal (cancellation; check the rate range); missed foetal beats (refractory period, averaging over several beats, rejecting an RR that is exactly double the average).
Check. A trace stuck at about 80 per minute is almost always the mother, since a foetal rate below 110 is itself a bradycardia; the monitor and the operator should confirm with the maternal pulse.

bank.q: A body plethysmograph is used to measure thoracic gas volume and airway resistance. Explain the principle with Boyle's law, derive the volume equation, and discuss why the panting manoeuvre is used.
outline: Patient sits in a sealed box and breathes through a shutter and mouthpiece
Shutter closes and the patient pants against it
Alveolar gas is compressed and rarefied, mouth pressure tracks alveolar pressure
Box pressure changes oppositely as box volume changes
Boyle's law: P1V1 = P2V2 applied to the gas in the chest and to the box
Thoracic gas volume obtained, residual volume = thoracic gas volume minus expiratory reserve volume
Shutter open, flow and box pressure, scaled by the closed-shutter slope, give airway resistance
Panting keeps gas exchange and temperature effects small
answer: Set-up. The subject sits in a rigid, sealed box of about 600 L and breathes through a mouthpiece that carries a shutter, a pneumotachometer and a mouth-pressure tap. A second transducer measures box pressure. A piston pump calibrates the box: a known volume change gives a known box-pressure change, Kbox (for example 400 mL per cm H₂O).

Closed shutter. At end-expiration (FRC) the shutter closes and the subject pants gently at about 1 Hz. There is no flow, so mouth pressure equals alveolar pressure. Each push compresses the trapped lung gas; the chest volume falls by ΔV and the box gas expands by the same ΔV, so box pressure falls slightly.

answer.text: Derivation. Boyle's law for the dry lung gas (the water vapour pressure stays 47 mmHg):
answer.pre:
P V = (P + ΔP)(V − ΔV)
P V = P V − P ΔV + ΔP V − ΔP ΔV
neglect ΔP ΔV (product of two small changes):
V = P ΔV / ΔP
V<sub>tg</sub> = ΔV × (P<sub>B</sub> − P<sub>H₂O</sub>) / ΔP<sub>mouth</sub>,   ΔV = K<sub>box</sub> × ΔP<sub>box</sub>

answer.text: Numbers.

answer: Open shutter: airway resistance. The subject pants through the pneumotachometer. To drive flow, alveolar pressure must differ from mouth pressure; the compression of alveolar gas shows as a box-pressure swing. The closed-shutter slope (ΔPmouth/ΔPbox = 9.7/0.075 = 129.3) converts box swing to alveolar pressure, so Raw = 129.3 × (ΔPbox/V̇). With 0.0116 cm H₂O of box swing per L/s: Raw = 1.50 cm H₂O per L/s, normal.

Why panting. (1) Small, fast swings keep the lung gas isothermal and saturated, so Boyle's law applies, while the box calibration at the same frequency covers the adiabatic box gas. (2) Panting holds the glottis open, so mouth pressure tracks alveolar pressure. (3) The box temperature drifts slowly (body heat, breath warmth); at 1 Hz this drift is negligible within each cycle. (4) Panting keeps the lung volume near FRC, so Vtg is measured at a known volume.

Limitations. The subject must cooperate and tolerate the closed box; cheek movement during panting lowers mouth pressure (cheeks are supported by the hands); severe obstruction can make mouth pressure lag alveolar pressure and over-read Vtg.
Evaluation. Unlike helium dilution, the box counts gas trapped behind closed airways, so it is the method of choice in COPD and gives airway resistance in the same sitting.
Check. RV/TLC = 1.8/5.8 = 0.31 lies in the normal 0.25–0.35 band, consistent with the normal Raw.

bank.q: Design a bedside monitoring chain for a post-operative patient that continuously shows ECG, SpO2, blood pressure and breathing. State what each channel measures, how alarms are set, and how artefacts are reduced.
outline: ECG electrodes with high common-mode rejection amplifier and driven right leg
SpO2 finger probe with ratio-of-ratios processing
Blood pressure by automated cuff, or arterial line if continuous values are needed
Respiration from chest impedance measured through the ECG electrodes
Alarm limits set from the patient's baseline with delay to avoid false calls
Artefacts: movement, mains interference, electrode drying, poor perfusion
Use of filters, averaging, lead-off detection and signal quality indicators
Isolation barrier for patient safety and defibrillation protection

answer.text: Overall chain. Four channels share one patient-side front end and one display/alarm processor, separated from mains by an isolation barrier:
answer.pre:
ECG electrodes ──┬─ ECG amplifier ─┐
                 └─ impedance (50 kHz) respiration ─┤
SpO₂ finger probe ── red/IR driver + photodiode ─────┤→ isolation → ADC → processor → display, trends, alarms
NIBP cuff ── pump, valve, pressure sensor ───────────┘

answer: ECG channel. Three or five electrodes; an instrumentation amplifier with high input impedance and common-mode rejection above about 100 dB; right-leg drive to reduce mains interference; monitoring bandwidth about 0.5–40 Hz to suppress baseline wander and muscle noise. Heart rate = 60/RR; QRS detection drives the rate and arrhythmia alarms. Lead-off detection uses a tiny DC or AC test current.

SpO₂ channel. Alternating 660/940 nm LEDs, photodiode, transimpedance amplifier, AC/DC separation, ratio of ratios R and the calibration curve (R = 0.55 gives about 96 %). It also gives pulse rate and a plethysmographic waveform, whose amplitude is a perfusion index.

Blood pressure. An automated oscillometric cuff every 5–15 minutes after surgery (MAP at maximum oscillation, systolic and diastolic from amplitude ratios). If the patient is unstable or on vasoactive drugs, an arterial line with a strain-gauge transducer zeroed at the right atrium gives beat-to-beat pressure.

Breathing. Transthoracic impedance through the ECG electrodes: a small 50 kHz current (well under 1 mA) and the voltage change of about 1 Ω per litre give respiratory rate and an apnoea alarm. Where opioid depression of breathing is the main risk, nasal capnography is added, because SpO₂ stays normal on oxygen while CO₂ rises.

answer.text: Alarm settings (typical adult, adjusted to the patient's own baseline).

answer: Artefact reduction. Motion: accelerometer or signal-quality index to hold alarms on obviously corrupted segments; averaging of SpO₂ over 4–8 s; R must show a matching pulse in both channels. Mains interference: right-leg drive, shielded leads, notch filter. Electrode drying: fresh gel electrodes daily, lead-off alarm. Cardiac artefact on the impedance signal: band-pass filter and a threshold above the heartbeat bump; cross-check that the breath rate differs from the heart rate. Poor perfusion: move the probe, warm the hand, use an ear or forehead sensor.

Signal processing and display. All channels are sampled after the isolation barrier (ECG at 250–500 samples per second, SpO₂ channels at a few hundred, impedance at about 50). The processor shows waveforms in real time, numbers updated every few seconds, and trends over 24 hours, so a slow fall in MAP or SpO₂ is seen before it crosses an alarm limit. A central station collects several bedsides over the hospital network.

Example check of the numbers. RR = 0.80 s gives 75 per minute, well inside 50–120; R = 0.55 gives about 96 %, above 90 %; a cuff reading of 128/82 gives MAP 97 mmHg, inside 65–110; 16 breaths per minute is inside 8–30. None of the alarms should sound for this patient.
Safety. Isolated (type CF) applied parts limit patient leakage current to about 10 µA, and defibrillation-proof inputs with series resistors and voltage clamps protect the amplifiers.

Evaluation. Alarm fatigue is the main real-world failure: limits based on the patient's baseline, short alarm delays and combined alarms (low SpO₂ with apnoea) keep the alarms meaningful. The design meets the brief: continuous ECG, SpO₂ and breathing, with intermittent or continuous pressure as the patient needs.

bank.q: Compare the pneumotachometer, the spirometer and the impedance method for measuring ventilation. Discuss accuracy, patient effort and suitability for long-term apnea monitoring.
outline: Pneumotachometer gives true flow from a pressure drop, needs a mouthpiece and is accurate but interferes with breathing
Spirometer integrates flow or volume directly, used for forced manoeuvres in the clinic
Impedance method needs only surface electrodes and gives a relative change, not absolute volume
Impedance is best for apnea alarm, not for lung function numbers
Movement and cardiac pulsation corrupt the impedance signal
Choice depends on whether absolute volume or a trend is needed
A 3 L syringe check is standard for spirometer and pneumotachograph chains
answer: What each measures. The spirometer measures volume (bell, rolling seal) or integrates flow (turbine) at the mouth; the pneumotachometer measures flow as a pressure drop across a laminar resistance and integrates it to volume; impedance pneumography measures the change in transthoracic impedance as the lungs fill.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: Feature
Spirometer
Pneumotachometer
Impedance
rows: only after calibration per patient; drifts with posture
full forced manoeuvre, mouthpiece, nose clip
mouthpiece or mask; adds a little resistance

answer: Accuracy in numbers. A spirometer reads 3.0 ± 0.09 L on the calibration syringe. A pneumotachometer with Rpt = 1.5 cm H₂O per L/s reads 0.5 L/s from 0.75 cm H₂O, but a 0.01 L/s zero offset integrates to 0.6 L per minute, so it needs per-breath reset. An impedance signal of 0.5 Ω for a 0.5 L breath can drift by tens of percent when the patient turns over.

Patient effort. Spirometry needs a cooperative subject who can perform a maximal blow; it is impossible in an infant or an unconscious patient. A pneumotachometer needs only a sealed mouthpiece or mask, so it suits ventilated patients but not a sleeping baby at home. Impedance needs nothing beyond electrodes, often the ECG electrodes already in place.

Suitability for long-term apnoea monitoring. Impedance is the practical choice: unobtrusive, cheap, and the alarm needs only the timing of breaths (no change above threshold for 10–20 s). Its weaknesses are obstructive apnoea, where the chest keeps moving against a closed airway and the impedance still changes, and cardiac artefact, which can look like shallow breathing. Adding SpO₂ and heart rate, or a nasal thermistor, covers these gaps.

Calibration in common. The 3 L syringe checks spirometer and pneumotachometer volume, emptied at several speeds to check the pneumotachometer's linearity; the impedance channel is checked by its own test resistance and is never used for litres.

Ventilators. In intensive care the pneumotachometer sits in the ventilator circuit at the patient Y-piece, measuring both directions; heated heads prevent condensation, and the integrated volume gives tidal volume and minute ventilation alarms. This is where the pneumotachometer, not the spirometer, does long-term monitoring.
Conclusion. Use the spirometer for diagnostic lung volumes, the pneumotachometer for flow in the laboratory and on ventilators, and impedance for continuous rate and apnoea watching.

glossary.def: Listening to body sounds, here the Korotkoff sounds over an artery below a cuff.
Automated cuff method that reads pressure from the size of the pressure pulsations in the cuff.
A diaphragm whose resistance changes when pressure bends it, used in direct blood pressure lines.
Volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, about 5 L/min at rest in an adult.
Blood flow equals the amount of a substance taken up per minute divided by the arteriovenous concentration difference.
A dye used for dilution cardiac output, measured optically because it absorbs near 800 nm.
The part of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles contract and eject blood.
The part of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles relax and fill.
The cup-shaped chest piece of a stethoscope, best for low-frequency sounds such as S3 and S4.
The flat chest piece of a stethoscope, which filters low frequencies and highlights murmurs.
Any abnormal rhythm, detected by comparing each RR interval with set limits.
Time between two successive R waves of the ECG, in milliseconds; inverse gives heart rate.
The baby's heart rate, normally about 110 to 160 beats per minute.
Instrument that records the volume of air breathed in and out and the speed of the breath.
A spirometer design in which a piston rolls on a flexible seal with low friction, giving an accurate volume signal.
Ambient temperature and pressure, saturated with water vapour; conditions at the spirometer itself.
The highest flow, in litres per minute, reached during a forced expiration.
Volume that can still be breathed out after a normal quiet expiration.
Method that finds lung volume from the dilution of a known amount of helium in a closed circuit.
Pressure inside the air sacs, equal to atmospheric when no air is moving.
A pause in breathing, commonly alarming when it lasts longer than about 10 to 20 seconds.
Optical recording of the pulsatile blood volume in a finger or earlobe.
At constant temperature, pressure times volume of a fixed amount of gas stays constant.
A sealed box in which pressure changes around a breathing subject give lung volume and airway resistance.
